Consider the arc of the curve $x=2y-{y}^{3}$ that lies in the first quadrant between its $y$-intercepts. What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?

Consider the arc of the curve $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡y$ that lies in the first quadrant between its $y$-intercept and the line $y=e.$ What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
feedback.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =0 \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡y} & ={e}^{0} \\ y & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $y=1$ to $y=e.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=\frac{1}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{1}{y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}y\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}\sqrt{{y}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$
